Instruments are all operating near their noise floor; variation is measurement noise, not signal
Temporal correlations exist but are obscured by phase shifts longer than the baseline window or by irregular sampling intervals
Baseline period is too short to resolve drift, and apparent independence is a sampling artifact
One or more instruments are malfunctioning or miscalibrated, producing noise unrelated to the intended measurand
Environmental or instrumental drift affecting resonator systems selectively began on day 20; pendulum systems are decoupled
The day-20 resonator_obs elevation is a statistical fluctuation within normal variance; all four instruments remain stable and independent

Resonator systems (lab and obs) are sensitive to a common physical driver (e.g., mechanical vibration, temperature) that began or changed on day 20; this driver is independent of the pendulum driver, explaining their lack of correlation

Sampling or trial assignment on day 20 introduced bias (e.g., different operator, different ambient condition during the day, or trials grouped by time-of-day effect); the elevation in resonator_obs is real but transient
Measurement error or data entry error in resonator_obs trials 217–234; values should be checked against raw instrument logs

Single-instrument environmental drift in resonator_obs began day 20; resonator_lab and pendulum systems decouple because they measure independent physical quantities or are thermally/vibrationally isolated from resonator_obs.
Day-20 resonator_obs elevation is a statistical fluctuation (n=18 trials) within expected noise; all four instruments remain genuinely independent and stable.

Sampling order or time-of-day effect on day 20 caused the elevation; trials were assigned in a non-random order (e.g., all pendulum_obs first, then resonator_obs), and an afternoon thermal or procedural drift affected only resonator_obs.
Data entry or calibration error in resonator_obs trials 217–234; raw instrument logs must be checked.

Resonator_obs and resonator_lab measure the same physical quantity but via instrument paths decoupled enough that a common environmental driver affects them out of phase or with a time delay; correlation is obscured by noise or lag.
Pendulum_obs experienced localized environmental drift beginning ~day 23; shift is real, instrument-specific, not laboratory-wide

Pendulum_obs and pendulum_lab measure via independent hardware paths; pendulum_obs apparatus has drifted thermally or mechanically, while pendulum_lab has not, explaining their persistent low cross-correlation and the day-23 shift in obs only

The day-23 shift in pendulum_obs is a statistical fluctuation in post-baseline noise; all four instruments remain genuinely independent and stable, with the apparent shift a result of random clustering in a small post-baseline cohort
Data entry or calibration error in pendulum_obs trials post-day-20; systematic offset or transducer recalibration applied without documentation

All four instruments remain uncorrelated because they measure fundamentally independent physical processes, environmental drivers, or employ apparatus in sufficiently isolated locations; no shared signal exists

Pendulum_obs apparatus experienced a real, localized environmental or mechanical drift beginning ~day 23; shift is persistent and instrument-specific, not a noise fluctuation or shared environmental effect.

Pendulum_obs and pendulum_lab measure via sufficiently independent hardware (different transducers, housings, or environmental couplings) that they respond decorrelatively to noise; the day-23 apparent shift in pendulum_obs is a real but transient clustering of readings, not indicative of apparatus failure.

A calibration error, transducer replacement, or decimal/unit offset was applied to pendulum_obs data post-day-20, creating a systematic step offset without documentation; raw logs and maintenance records must be audited to rule out this pathway.

All four instruments measure sufficiently independent physical processes or are physically isolated such that no shared environmental driver or common signal propagates across the settlement; zero cross-correlation is expected and reflects genuine independence, not instrumental failure.

Residual: Something unconsidered—e.g., a shared environmental driver with a long time constant (>12 days) that decorrelates the instruments by introducing phase shifts or differential delays; a non-linear coupling between instruments; or a data-processing artifact (e.g., lag-correction or interpolation applied post-hoc to one stream).

Pendulum_obs apparatus experienced a real, localized instrumental drift beginning ~day 23; shift is persistent, unidirectional, and specific to this hardware path, not a noise fluctuation or shared environmental effect.

Pendulum_obs and pendulum_lab measure via sufficiently independent hardware that they decorrelate naturally; the observed shift in pendulum_obs is a real but statistically modest clustering of readings into the lower half of the natural noise distribution, not indicative of apparatus failure or systematic drift.

A calibration error, transducer replacement, or systematic offset was applied to pendulum_obs data post-day-20, creating a persistent step shift without documentation; raw logs and maintenance records must be audited to rule out this pathway.

All four instruments measure sufficiently independent physical processes or occupy sufficiently isolated hardware environments such that no shared environmental driver propagates across settlement; zero cross-correlation is expected and reflects genuine independence, not instrumental failure. The pendulum_obs drift is an instrument-specific response to a localized environmental change decoupled from lab instruments.

A higher-order explanation: a common environmental driver with a long time constant (>12 days) or non-linear coupling affects all four instruments but decorrelates them via phase shifts, time delays, or differential frequency responses; alternatively, a data-processing artifact (lag-correction, interpolation, or quantization) was applied post-hoc to one or more streams and artificially obscured correlation.

Pendulum_obs apparatus experienced a real, persistent instrumental drift beginning ~day 23; shift is hardware-specific (transducer, optical alignment, or mount), not environmental or noise-driven, and independent from pendulum_lab via separate detection paths.

The persistent downward shift in pendulum_obs is a transient clustering of readings into the lower half of the noise distribution—statistically rare but explainable by noise—and does not indicate apparatus failure.
A calibration event, transducer replacement, or systematic offset was applied to pendulum_obs post-day 20, creating a step-function shift that was not documented in settlement records or my own logs.

All four instruments measure independent physical processes or occupy sufficiently isolated hardware environments that zero cross-correlation is expected; the pendulum_obs drift is a hardware-specific environmental response (mount settling, thermal coupling, optical drift) decoupled from lab instruments.

A higher-order explanation: a common environmental driver with non-linear coupling, phase shifts, or time delays affects all four instruments but decorrelates them via differential frequency responses; alternatively, a post-hoc data-processing artifact (smoothing, lag-correction, interpolation, or quantization) obscured correlation without documentation.
